indicators.note: the choir and its ceasing are put through a performance, so these letters are worked into a fresh order

explanation.surface: The church singers have stopped their performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb inviting you to look, but it is the noun for a bishop's area. 'performing' rearranges CHOIRCEASED.
explanation.definitionFit: A see is the district under a bishop's authority, and the larger one ruled by an archbishop carries this name.

definitions.meaning: verb: stays put, is left behind
what is left after burning, especially a body after cremation

explanation.walkthrough: 'to see' is only a link joining the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Stays as a verb means is left over; as a noun, leftover ashes or a corpse are the departed's mortal relics.

indicators.note: something broadcast is scattered widely, so these letters are spread and resown in a new order

explanation.surface: A rough-and-ready episode of the sitcom Dad's Army went out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a British TV comedy about the WWII volunteer defence force of older men; 'broadcast' fits the TV picture but rearranges MADEROUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: The wartime volunteer force of older British men was nicknamed after the fathers who filled it, as in the famous sitcom.

parts.note: the setter speaking of himself says I'm, short for I am
old age, so simply age

explanation.surface: A portrait of the crossword compiler in dotage.
explanation.definitionFit: A likeness or representation, such as a photograph or painting, is a synonym of picture.

clue.text: Don't come it or you're in trouble!

definitions.text: Don't come it or you're in trouble!

parts.words: Don't come it or you're in trouble!
parts.note: reads like a warning not to try it on; cryptically 'come it' points to the idiom 'come a ...' meaning take a heavy fall or fail badly

explanation.surface: A stern warning not to cheek someone or there will be consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come it' is British slang for showing off or being cheeky; the hidden reading is the idiom of coming to grief.
explanation.definitionFit: To come a cropper is an idiom for falling heavily or failing, so not coming one keeps you out of trouble.

parts.note: rendered a song means sang it

indicators.note: tells us to read the word for the tune from right to left

parts.note: an air is a tune

explanation.surface: Someone sang a song in reverse after a few glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rendered' suggests a translation, but it means performed vocally; 'backwards' turns the tune word round, and 'after' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish punch of red wine and fruit, served as a summer drink.

indicators.note: the word for left sits inside the word for debate

parts.note: comment, discussion of a matter, stands in for debate
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: How a left-wing member conducts themselves during a debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks political but is the nautical side, PORT.
explanation.definitionFit: Comportment is formal for conduct or bearing, the way one carries oneself.

clue.text: Good man's come down with overwork

parts.note: a saint, abbreviated St, is a good man in crosswords
rain comes down from the sky

explanation.surface: A virtuous man has collapsed through doing too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive exertion puts a tax on body or mind, so overwork can be a synonym.

clue.text: Model one found in plump old lady

indicators.note: the numeral is located inside the other pieces put together

parts.note: to plump for something is to opt for it
slang for one's mother, mum
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A fashion model has turned up in the shape of a plump elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plump' looks like an adjective for the old lady, but it is the verb meaning choose, OPT.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, model means ideal or best possible, the sense of the Latin-derived word.

clue.text: Stood at the bar, say, more or less

definitions.meaning: what someone stands in a pub: drinks for the whole group, as one example

explanation.walkthrough: In British pubs you 'stand' a round of drinks, paying for everyone; 'say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying a set of drinks is standing 'a round'; and approximately, give or take, is the adverb sense.

definitions.note: a Freemason's leader: the head of a Masonic lodge or order

indicators.note: the letters of arms and granted are made different by being reordered

explanation.surface: Permission has been given for a pub called the Mason's Arms, though it differs from usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mason's Arms' looks like a pub name; split it, so 'arms' is fodder with GRANTED, and 'Mason's' defines a Masonic chief.
explanation.definitionFit: Freemasonry's lodges and grand lodges are headed by an officer bearing this title, also used for chess masters.

clue.text: Going on patrol, initially, with sailor

indicators.note: only the opening letter of patrol is wanted

parts.note: a rating is a non-commissioned sailor

explanation.surface: Heading out on a patrol in company with a seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: To prate is to chatter on idly, so going on, talking at length, is this participle.

clue.text: Nero, perhaps, right after exercise in ruined Rome

indicators.note: the exercise and right letters go inside the scrambled city
the city's name is wrecked, so its letters are scrambled
the letter for right comes after the exercise letters

parts.note: PE, physical education, is exercise

explanation.surface: Nero did right after exercising while Rome lay in ruins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' scrambles the city name; 'in' puts the exercise-plus-right letters inside it, splitting it two and two.
explanation.definitionFit: Nero was a Roman ruler, an example of an imperial sovereign; 'perhaps' signals the example.

definitions.meaning: payments made for a home or flat

explanation.surface: People share their accommodation bills.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear in cloth is a rip; and tenants pay these regular sums to a landlord.

clue.text: Make out traces in a design

indicators.note: the letters are designed afresh, rearranged into a new pattern

explanation.surface: Someone tries to discern faint lines inside a pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make out' looks like a phrase about kissing or seeing, but means establish; 'design' is a verb-like signal to rework the letters into SCERTAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To make out is to discover or determine, to establish with certainty.

clue.text: Disposal of last atom in life?

definitions.text: Disposal of last atom in life?

parts.words: Disposal of last atom in life?
parts.note: a whimsical scientific take on a funeral rite: burning a body so that its final particles of life are disposed of

explanation.surface: A physicist wonders how the final particle of a living thing is got rid of.
explanation.definitionFit: Burning a corpse is a way of disposing of the dead and every last bit of them.

indicators.note: in an across clue the handle is placed on, that is after, the motorway piece

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway; with the 's it gives MIS, using 1 as I
a CB radio user's call name is a handle

explanation.surface: A CB radio call sign heard on the motorway is a muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the London-to-Leeds motorway, with 1 read as I; CB radio users go by nicknames called handles.
explanation.definitionFit: To fluff is to bungle or botch, as an actor fluffs a line.

clue.text: Dress up in small, small number

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as in clothing sizes
wee is Scottish for small
ten is a number

explanation.surface: Getting dressed up in a tiny size.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something more pleasant or attractive, sugaring it, is a figurative synonym for dressing it up.

clue.text: Everyone, for example, has half roll on fast

parts.note: all means everyone

indicators.note: only the front half of the word roll is wanted

explanation.surface: Everyone, including one person here, gets half a bread roll before fasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like going without food but is the musical tempo.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical tempo marking meaning quick and lively, from Italian.

indicators.note: the word the loses its final letter

parts.note: rum is a drink

explanation.surface: The excitement comes from never-ending drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: A continuous droning or humming sound is a buzz.

indicators.note: removes the first letter of the word for tart

parts.note: a strumpet is old slang for a tart, a prostitute

explanation.surface: Some money comes from a semi-naked prostitute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brass' looks like British slang for money (or for a prostitute), but means brass instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass in an orchestra means its metal wind instruments, of which this is one.

indicators.note: the run of letters is taken from inside the phrase Iran dominates

explanation.surface: Iran takes a gamble in dominating the region.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, chance means haphazard or unplanned.

indicators.note: the word is not quite complete, so its last letter goes

parts.note: needless means unnecessary

explanation.surface: Gratuitous jibes that are nearly pointless.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or goad them, so the verb in the third person matches.

definitions.meaning: a bar or brace in a framework

explanation.definitionFit: A structural brace is a bar in a framework; to walk proudly with swagger is the verb sense.

parts.note: seems to describe someone gone to bed; at Oxford or Cambridge one is 'up' while studying, so this is a former student

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a man has gone to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: British universities say students 'go up' and are 'up' while in residence; a graduate is no longer up.
explanation.definitionFit: A graduate or former pupil of a school or university.

indicators.note: the word for stumble goes without the gravity letter

parts.note: to stagger is to stumble
g is the symbol for gravity's acceleration

explanation.surface: A thespian trips because of weightlessness.
explanation.definitionFit: A stager is a performer on stage, as in 'old stager' for a veteran.

parts.note: a little horror is a naughty child, an imp
lore is a body of traditional stories

explanation.surface: Asking to be told scary tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horror' suggests scary stories, but a 'little horror' is a mischievous child.
explanation.definitionFit: To entreat or plead earnestly is a stronger synonym for beg.

clue.text: A French lot taking a time to make miserable

parts.note: un is French for a

indicators.note: the word for lot takes in the two letters

parts.note: one's lot in life is one's fortune
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French group has a hard time and is made miserable.
explanation.definitionFit: Wretched and unhappy or unlucky are near synonyms, both meaning in a sorry state.
